title: Conditions and exit codes
goal: Make scripts decide: test files, strings and numbers, choose with case, and return exit codes that CI tools understand.
setup: # P1: a release folder in different states
# P3: disk usage numbers from 4 servers
# P5: a broken health check script

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Check that the log folder exists and that the last HTTP code is 200.' '# Optional argument: number of retries (warn if more than 3).' 'LOG_DIR=logs' 'CODE=$(cat last-code.txt)' 'RETRIES=$1' 'if [ -f "$LOG_DIR" ]; then echo "log folder OK"; else echo "log folder MISSING"; fi' 'if ["$CODE" = "200"]; then echo "HTTP OK"; else echo "HTTP FAIL"; fi' 'if [ $RETRIES -gt 3 ]; then echo "warning: $RETRIES retries"; fi' > health.sh
printf '%s\n' 'INFO start' 'ERROR disk full' 'INFO stop' > app.log

warmup.q: What is the difference between `'$HOME'` and `"$HOME"`?
warmup.a: Single quotes print `$HOME` literally. Double quotes replace it with `/home/wicky`.

warmup.q: A child script cannot see `DB_HOST`. What is missing?
warmup.a: `export DB_HOST`. Only exported variables are passed to child processes.
stderr is sent to the screen (where stdout was at that moment), then stdout moves to the file. Correct: `cmd > file 2>&1`.

warmup.q: Which `xargs` option runs one command per input line, putting the line at `{}`?
warmup.a: `-I{}`, for example `xargs -I{} echo docker pull {} < images.txt`.

problems.title: Pre-deploy checks with file tests
problems.situation: Before every deploy, a script must check the release folder: the config exists and is not empty, the logs folder exists, the deploy script can run, and the lock file is empty. If one check fails, the deploy must stop.
task: In `release`, write a script `check.sh` (or type the lines directly) that tests each item below and prints `OK` or `FAIL`.
`app.yml` is a regular file (`-f`) and not empty (`-s`).
`logs` is a folder (`-d`), and it is writable (`-w`).
`deploy.sh` is executable (`-x`). `empty.lock` exists (`-e`) but is empty (`! -s`).
Count the failures and finish with `exit 1` if there is at least one.
hints: Pattern: `if [ -f app.yml ]; then echo "OK ..."; else echo "FAIL ..."; fi`.
`!` means not: `[ ! -s empty.lock ]` is true when the file is empty.
Use a counter: `FAILS=0`, and in the else part `FAILS=$((FAILS + 1))`. At the end: `[ "$FAILS" -eq 0 ] || exit 1`.
solution: if [ "$@" ]; then echo "OK   $msg"; else echo "FAIL $msg"; FAILS=$((FAILS + 1)); fi

explanation.meaning: Regular file / folder (directory) / exists (any type).
File exists and its size is more than 0.
The current user can read / write / execute it.
`!` negates the test: true when the file is empty.
Runs the test with the remaining arguments. A small function keeps the script short (Day 9).
Tell the caller (Jenkins, cron, another script) that the checks failed.

problems.expected_output:
OK   app.yml is a file
OK   app.yml is not empty
OK   logs is a folder
OK   logs is writable
FAIL deploy.sh is executable
OK   empty.lock exists
OK   empty.lock is empty
failures: 1
exit code: 1
OK   app.yml is a file
OK   app.yml is not empty
OK   logs is a folder
OK   logs is writable
OK   deploy.sh is executable
OK   empty.lock exists
OK   empty.lock is empty
failures: 0
exit code: 0
mistakes: Using `-f` on a folder: `[ -f logs ]` is false, because `logs` is a directory. Use `-d`, or `-e` for "any type".
No spaces inside the brackets: `[-f app.yml]` gives `bash: [-f: command not found`.
Printing FAIL but ending with exit code 0. Jenkins then shows the step as green.
problems.interview_say: I test files with `-f` for a file, `-d` for a folder, `-e` for exists, `-s` for not empty, and `-r -w -x` for permissions. If a check fails, the script ends with a non-zero exit code so the pipeline stops.
problems.try_yourself: Add a check that `app.yml` is newer than `deploy.sh`: `[ app.yml -nt deploy.sh ]`.

problems.title: [ ] vs [[ ]]: empty variables and patterns
problems.situation: A Jenkins job prints `[: =: unary operator expected` when the `BRANCH` variable is empty. The team also wants to deploy only branches that start with `release/`. `[[ ]]` solves both problems.
task: Set `BRANCH=` (empty). Run `[ $BRANCH = main ] && echo yes`. Read the error.
Run the same test with quotes: `[ "$BRANCH" = main ]`. Then with `[[ $BRANCH = main ]]`.
Set `BRANCH=release/2.4`. Test the pattern `[[ $BRANCH == release/* ]]`.
Check the version format with a regex: `[[ $VERSION =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]]` for `2.4.1` and `2.4`.
Combine two tests inside `[[ ]]` with `&&`.
hints: With an empty unquoted variable, `[ $BRANCH = main ]` becomes `[ = main ]`. One word is missing.
`[[ ]]` is a bash keyword: it does not split variables, and it supports `==` patterns and `=~` regex.
In `[[ ]]`, do not quote the right side of a pattern, or it is compared as plain text.
solution: [ $BRANCH = main ] && echo yes || echo "test failed, exit code: $?"
[ "$BRANCH" = main ] || echo "quoted [ ]: no error, just false"
[[ $BRANCH = main ]] || echo "[[ ]]: no error, just false"
if [[ $BRANCH == release/* ]]; then echo "deploy $BRANCH to staging"; fi
if [[ $VERSION =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]]; then echo "$VERSION: valid"; else echo "$VERSION: invalid"; fi

explanation.meaning: `[` got `= main` with nothing on the left, because the empty variable vanished. Exit code 2 = error in the test.
Quotes keep an empty value as one empty word. Always quote inside `[ ]`.
Bash keyword. Variables are not split, so quotes are optional on the left side.
Pattern match (like file wildcards) inside `[[ ]]` only.
Regular expression match. `^` start, `$` end, `[0-9]+` one or more digits, `\.` a real dot.
String is not empty / is empty.

problems.expected_output:
bash: [: =: unary operator expected
test failed, exit code: 2
quoted [ ]: no error, just false
[[ ]]: no error, just false
deploy release/2.4 to staging
2.4.1: valid
2.4: invalid
feature or release branch
mistakes: `[ $BRANCH = main ]` with empty BRANCH: `bash: [: =: unary operator expected`.
Quoting the pattern: `[[ $BRANCH == "release/*" ]]` compares with the text `release/*` and is false.
Using `[[ ]]` in a script run by `sh script.sh`: `sh` (dash) gives `[[: not found`. Run it with `bash`.

checks.run: printf '[[ a == a ]] && echo ok\n' > t.sh; sh t.sh

problems.interview_say: `[ ]` is the old test command, so I must quote variables. `[[ ]]` is a bash keyword: it handles empty variables safely and supports patterns and regex. In bash scripts I prefer `[[ ]]`.

problems.title: Disk alert: number tests and elif
problems.situation: The monitoring team wants a simple rule for each server: 90% or more is CRITICAL, 80% or more is WARNING, else OK. The numbers are in `disk-usage.txt` (server name, then percent).
task: Read the file line by line with `while read -r host pct`.
Use `if`, `elif`, `else` with number tests (`-ge`) to print the level for each server.
Count the CRITICAL servers and print the count at the end.
Read the Mistakes part: why `[ 9 > 10 ]` is dangerous.
hints: For numbers use `-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge`. `=` and `!=` are for strings.
Test the biggest limit first: `if [ "$pct" -ge 90 ]; then ... elif [ "$pct" -ge 80 ]; then ... else ... fi`.
Inside `(( ))` normal math works: `(( pct >= 90 ))`.

explanation.meaning: Read each line; the first word goes to `host`, the rest to `pct`.
Greater than or equal, for whole numbers.
"else if": checked only when the first test was false.
Formatted print: `%-9s` text left-aligned in 9 characters, `%%` prints a real `%`.
Arithmetic test. True (exit 0) when the math result is not zero.

problems.expected_output:
web-01     45%  OK
web-02     85%  WARNING
db-01      92%  CRITICAL
cache-01    9%  OK
critical servers: 1
page the on-call engineer
mistakes: `[ 9 > 10 ]` is not a comparison. `>` is a redirect: it creates a file called `10`, and the test is true.
Using `-gt` with text: `[ OK -gt 5 ]` gives `bash: [: OK: integer expression expected`.
Testing 80 before 90: then 92 matches the WARNING branch first and never becomes CRITICAL.
problems.interview_say: For numbers I use `-gt`, `-ge`, `-lt` and so on, or `(( ))`. In single brackets `>` is a redirect, not a comparison. I check the highest threshold first in an if/elif chain.
problems.try_yourself: Run `[ 9 > 10 ] && echo true; ls`. Do you see a file named `10`? Remove it with `rm 10`.

head: Numbers
Strings
Meaning
rows: less or equal / greater or equal

problems.title: case: one script for dev, staging and prod
problems.situation: The team has one deploy script for all environments. The first argument decides the server and the number of replicas. Many `if/elif` lines are hard to read; `case` is clearer.
task: Write `deploy-env.sh` that uses `case "$1" in ... esac`.
`dev` or `development`: 1 replica on `dev.local`. `staging`: 2 replicas. `prod` or `production`: 4 replicas, and print a warning.
Any other value: print a usage message to stderr and `exit 2`.
Run it with `dev`, `prod`, `test`, and with no argument. Print the exit code each time.
hints: Each branch ends with `;;`. Use `|` for two names: `dev|development)`.
`*)` matches everything else. Put it last.
Usage to stderr: `echo "usage: $0 dev|staging|prod" >&2`.
solution: for env in dev prod test ""; do

explanation.meaning: Compare the value with each pattern from top to bottom.
`|` means or: either word matches.
End of a branch. Bash jumps to `esac`.
Default branch: anything that did not match before.
Send this message to stderr. Errors and usage messages belong there.
By habit, 2 means "wrong usage"; 1 means a general error.

problems.expected_output:
--- arg: 'dev'
deploy to dev.local with 1 replicas
exit code: 0
--- arg: 'prod'
WARNING: deploying to production
deploy to prod.local with 4 replicas
exit code: 0
--- arg: 'test'
usage: deploy-env.sh dev|staging|prod
exit code: 2
--- arg: ''
usage: deploy-env.sh dev|staging|prod
exit code: 2
mistakes: Forgetting `;;`: bash stops with `syntax error near unexpected token` and points at the `)` of the next pattern.
Putting `*)` first: it matches everything, so the other branches never run.
Ending with `fi` instead of `esac`. A `case` block always closes with `esac` (case backwards).

checks.run:
printf 'case x in
 a) echo a
 b) echo b ;;
esac
' > c.sh; bash c.sh

problems.interview_say: I use `case` when one value decides between many options, like the environment name. Each pattern ends with `;;`, and `*)` handles wrong input with a usage message and exit code 2.
problems.try_yourself: Add a branch `[0-9]*)` that prints "numbers are not environments". Test with `bash deploy-env.sh 42`.

problems.title: Find the bug: the health check script
problems.situation: `health.sh` should say `log folder OK` and `HTTP OK`, and warn when the retries argument is more than 3. It prints `MISSING`, shows strange errors, and fails when no argument is given.
task: Run `bash health.sh` (no argument). Read the output and the errors.
Find 3 bugs: a wrong file test, a missing space, and an empty variable.
Fix them. Use `${RETRIES:-0}` to give a default value of 0.
Run `bash health.sh` and `bash health.sh 5`.
hints: `logs` is a folder, not a file.
`[` is a command. It needs a space after it, like any command.
With no argument, `$RETRIES` is empty: `[ -gt 3 ]`. A default and quotes fix it.
solution: # Check that the log folder exists and that the last HTTP code is 200.
# Optional argument: number of retries (warn if more than 3).
if [ -d "$LOG_DIR" ]; then echo "log folder OK"; else echo "log folder MISSING"; fi
if [ "$CODE" = "200" ]; then echo "HTTP OK"; else echo "HTTP FAIL"; fi

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: `logs` is a folder, so `-f` was false and printed MISSING.
Bug 2: no space after `[`. Bash looked for a command named `[200`.
Bug 3: use `0` when `$1` is empty or missing. Plus quotes around `$RETRIES`.

problems.expected_output:
log folder MISSING
health.sh: line 8: [200: command not found
HTTP FAIL
health.sh: line 9: [: -gt: unary operator expected
--- fixed, no argument ---
log folder OK
HTTP OK
--- fixed, 5 retries ---
log folder OK
HTTP OK
warning: 5 retries
mistakes: The error `health.sh: line 8: [200: command not found` looks like a problem with the number 200. It is really the missing space.
`[ -gt 3 ]` with an empty variable: `health.sh: line 9: [: -gt: unary operator expected`.
problems.interview_say: `[` is a command, so it needs spaces around it. I give arguments default values with `${1:-0}` and always quote variables in tests.
problems.try_yourself: Put `abc` in `last-code.txt`, and change the test to `-eq 200`. Run it. Read the new error.

problems.title: Exit codes that CI understands
problems.situation: Jenkins and GitHub Actions decide green or red only from the exit code of each step. The user learns the common codes and how to return them.
task: Run `true; echo $?` and `false; echo $?`.
Run a missing command `nosuchcmd; echo $?` and a non-executable file `./app.log; echo $?`.
Run `bash -c 'exit 3'; echo $?` and `bash -c 'exit 300'; echo $?`.
Use `grep -q` (quiet) as a test: `grep -q ERROR app.log && echo "errors found"`.
hints: 0 = success. 1 = general error. 2 = wrong usage.
126 = found but not executable. 127 = command not found. 130 = stopped with Ctrl+C.
Exit codes are 0-255. 300 becomes 300 - 256 = 44.
solution: grep -q ERROR app.log && echo "errors found (grep -q prints nothing, only sets the code)"

explanation.meaning: Success.
General failure (for example `false`, or `grep` found nothing).
Cannot execute (permission) / command not found.
Only 8 bits: the code is taken modulo 256.
Quiet: no output, only the exit code (0 = found).

problems.expected_output:
true:  0
false: 1
bash: nosuchcmd: command not found
missing command: 127
bash: ./app.log: Permission denied
not executable: 126
exit 3:   3
exit 300: 44
errors found (grep -q prints nothing, only sets the code)
mistakes: Ending a failing script with `echo "failed"` only. `echo` succeeds, so the exit code is 0 and CI shows green. Add `exit 1`.
Using `exit -1`. It becomes 255 and confuses people. Use small positive numbers.
problems.interview_say: CI tools look only at the exit code: 0 is success, anything else fails the step. My scripts use `exit 1` for errors, 2 for wrong usage, and `grep -q` or `test` for checks.
problems.try_yourself: Run `sleep 30`, press `Ctrl+C`, then `echo $?`. You should see 130.

problems.title: One-line checks with && and ||
problems.situation: Short guard lines are common at the top of scripts: create a folder only if missing, stop if a tool is not installed, print a message only if errors exist.
task: Create `backup` only if it does not exist: `[ -d backup ] || mkdir backup`.
Check a tool: `command -v kubectl >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "kubectl is not installed"`.
Print a message only if the log has errors: `grep -q ERROR app.log && echo "alert: errors in app.log"`.
Use a guard with exit: `[ -f app.yml ] || { echo "no app.yml" >&2; exit 1; }` inside `bash -c`.
hints: `A || B`: B runs only when A fails. `A && B`: B runs only when A works.
`command -v name` returns 0 when the command exists.
Group several commands after `||` with `{ ...; }`.
solution: command -v kubectl >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "kubectl is not installed"
grep -q ERROR app.log && echo "alert: errors in app.log"
bash -c '[ -f app.yml ] || { echo "no app.yml, stopping" >&2; exit 1; }; echo "never printed"'

explanation.meaning: Make the folder only if the test fails. (`mkdir -p` does the same in one step.)
Check if a tool exists, hide all output.
Print only when grep finds something.
Guard clause: stop the script early with an error.

problems.expected_output:
backup
kubectl is not installed
alert: errors in app.log
no app.yml, stopping
guard exit code: 1
problems.output_note: If `kubectl` is installed on the user's machine, that line prints nothing.
mistakes: Writing `|| echo "error"; exit 1` without braces: `exit 1` runs always, also on success.
Forgetting `>/dev/null 2>&1` with `command -v`: the path is printed when the tool exists.
problems.interview_say: I start scripts with guard lines like `command -v docker >/dev/null || { echo "docker missing" >&2; exit 1; }`, so the script fails early with a clear message.
problems.try_yourself: Rewrite the `kubectl` line as an `if ! command -v kubectl ...; then ... fi` block. Which one is easier to read for you?

interview.q: What is the difference between `[ ]` and `[[ ]]`?
interview.a: `[ ]` is the test command (POSIX), so variables must be quoted. `[[ ]]` is a bash keyword: it is safe with empty variables and supports patterns `==` and regex `=~`.

interview.q: How do you check if a file exists and is not empty?
interview.a: `[ -s file ]`. Use `-f` for a regular file, `-d` for a folder, and `-e` for any type.

interview.q: How do you compare numbers in bash?
interview.a: With `-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge` inside `[ ]`, or with normal operators inside `(( ))`, for example `(( count > 5 ))`.

interview.q: What does exit code 127 mean? And 126?
interview.a: 127: command not found. 126: the file was found but cannot be executed (for example no `x` permission).

interview.q: When do you use `case` instead of `if`?
interview.a: When one value is compared with many options, like an environment name or a command argument. It is shorter and easier to read.

recap.meaning: Run code depending on a test
End the script with an exit code
Quiet grep: only the exit code
Check that a tool is installed
